name: Question 5
problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

Question 5
?

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=1. Given that the point P(1,0,−1) lies on C, and that fy=xexy−2cos⁡y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
−j+2k
b
−j+k
c
j+k
d
2j−3k
e
−2j+k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=1. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(1,0).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (1,0):

fy(1,0)=1⋅e1⋅0−2cos⁡0=1⋅1−2⋅1=−1

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(1,0)=fy(1,0)(y−0)z−(−1)=(−1)yz=−y−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,0,−1) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=1z=−y−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=1, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=−y−1 (or y+z+1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,1,1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,1,1⟩=ijk100011=−j+k

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is −j+k.
